data.title: Molluscum contagiosum — viva
data.summary: Viral infections · 11 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Molluscum contagiosum** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is molluscum contagiosum?**
- Common benign self-limiting infection of the epidermis by molluscum contagiosum virus (poxvirus, genus Molluscipoxvirus; MCV-1 commonest, MCV-2 more in adults/HIV)
- Largest DNA virus pathogenic to humans; replicates in the cytoplasm

**Q2. Who gets it and how does it spread?**
- Children (direct contact, shared towels, swimming pools), sexually active adults (genital/pubic area), immunosuppressed (HIV, transplant) and atopic children
- Autoinoculation by scratching (Koebner) and shaving

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- Firm, smooth, pearly white or skin-coloured dome-shaped papules 2–5 mm with central umbilication; cheesy core can be expressed
- Children: trunk, flexures, face, limbs; adults: genitals, thighs, lower abdomen
- Giant molluscum (>1 cm), and many facial lesions — think HIV (CD4 <100)
- Molluscum dermatitis (eczema around lesions), 'BOTE' sign — inflamed lesions (Beginning Of The End) signalling regression

**Q4. What are molluscum bodies?**
- Large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson–Paterson bodies) in the keratinocytes of a lobulated, cup-shaped, endophytic epidermal proliferation
- Seen on squash smear of the expressed core (Giemsa/Wright) or biopsy

**Q5. Differential diagnosis?**
- Warts (no umbilication), milia, syringoma, sebaceous hyperplasia (adults, face), keratoacanthoma and BCC (single large lesion), epidermoid cyst
- In HIV: cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, penicilliosis (talaromycosis) — umbilicated papules on face; must do smear/biopsy
- Varicella (early), juvenile xanthogranuloma, Spitz naevus

**Q6. How do you investigate?**
- Clinical (dermoscopy shows central white-yellow polylobular structure with crown of peripheral vessels)
- Squash preparation for molluscum bodies; biopsy for atypical lesions
- In adults with genital lesions — screen for HIV and other STIs; in extensive facial lesions — HIV test

**Q7. Treatment options.**
- Watchful waiting in children (usually clears in 6–18 months; immunity develops)
- Physical: curettage, enucleation/expression with a needle (with topical anaesthetic), cryotherapy, electrocautery, laser (pulsed dye)
- Chemical: 10–20% KOH solution, cantharidin 0.7% (FDA-approved for molluscum in 2023), podophyllotoxin (adults, not in pregnancy), tretinoin, salicylic acid, trichloroacetic acid; berdazimer gel (nitric oxide donor, FDA 2024)
- Imiquimod is no longer favoured in children (trials showed no benefit)
- HIV: ART (immune reconstitution clears them); cidofovir in refractory

**Q8. Why treat genital molluscum in adults?**
- To prevent sexual transmission and autoinoculation, and it signals sexual exposure (screen for STIs)

**Q9. What is the course and prognosis?**
- Each lesion lasts ~2 months; the infection lasts months to years; heals without scars unless treated aggressively or secondarily infected
- Recurrence common; immunosuppressed — persistent, extensive lesions

**Q10. What is molluscum dermatitis and how do you manage it?**
- Eczematous patch around molluscum lesions (often signals immune response); treat with mild topical steroid/emollient; it often precedes clearance

**Q11. Which poxviruses affect human skin?**
- Molluscipoxvirus — molluscum contagiosum
- Orthopoxvirus — smallpox (eradicated), vaccinia, cowpox, mpox (monkeypox — 2022 global outbreak; umbilicated pustules on genitals, lymphadenopathy, tecovirimat)
- Parapoxvirus — orf, milker's nodule
- Yatapoxvirus — tanapox

## Quick spotter facts
- Pearly umbilicated papules with cheesy core — molluscum
- Henderson–Paterson bodies (molluscum bodies)
- Many giant facial mollusca — test for HIV; rule out cryptococcosis/histoplasmosis

## Note
Cantharidin (2023) and berdazimer (2024) approvals are newer than the textbooks — please confirm before using in a viva.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
